We've seen countless examples proving that giving Meta's Muse app full disk access on a Mac is an extraordinarily bad idea, and now another major privacy issue has emerged: someone discovered that Muse analyzes your communications and those of everyone around you every single hour.

Apple has expressed concern about this matter, stating in a blog post that it will introduce additional controls for the "Full Disk Access" feature that caused this problem……

Meta's Muse app makes this matter urgent

Meta recently launched the Muse personal AI agent app for iPhone and Mac. Although fully opening up all the data on your Apple device to a Meta app is clearly extremely unwise, the app quickly shot to the top of the App Store charts.

Sure enough, serious problems began emerging before long, and the situation has not improved. Wired reported that security researcher Karan Joshi found that Meta instructed Muse to harvest all the data needed to build a complete map of every relationship in a user's life.

One of Muse's instructions appeared to be to create a "dedicated page" for "every person in the user's life." According to its instructions, this hourly process collects information about family members, partners, friends, colleagues, "collaborators," and people the user "follows"……the instructions state: "where they live, what they do for work, topics they often discuss (moving houses, savings goals)." The instructions also add that the model can record "important dates," such as birthdays or anniversaries. A person's history can include contextual details, such as "the trip in March," "the argument that was already resolved," "last week's milestone."

Apple tightens Full Disk Access controls

You might think the prompt explaining to users on a Mac what granting an app Full Disk Access entails is clear enough, but it appears that's not the case. Even tech-savvy users hand over this all-access pass without truly realizing how dangerous this step is.

Apple said this feature was originally designed for backup applications, but developers later found more uses for it, including AI agents. The company said it intends to "introduce additional controls" to ensure users truly understand what they are doing when granting this permission.

What Apple must and must not do

Apple says this step is "essential," and I completely agree. When existing permission requests clearly fail to adequately convey the gravity of what is being granted, Apple must ensure users truly understand what they are allowing.

What I'd like to see is clearer, more explicit wording that discourages users from acting rashly before they truly understand the consequences. Roughly as follows:

Basically, the wording cannot be too strong. If a one-time confirmation could be done for apps that have already been granted this permission, I'd be happy to accept that.

Peter's popular comments

Although Apple occasionally asks whether I want to continue allowing apps to access location services, which I find somewhat annoying, I do appreciate this arrangement. Because at least once or twice I realized I didn't want a particular app to have that level of access anymore. It also reminds me to periodically think about which apps might be using my location data.

However, Apple absolutely must not repeat the mistake it made with the screen recording feature in macOS Sequoia. Although this feature is equally extremely dangerous and should carry very strong warnings, what Apple did was force us to confirm these permissions every week, and then confirm again every time we restart.

This approach was widely criticized as turning macOS into Microsoft Vista, and imposing on users a "subscription you didn't buy and can't cancel." In my view, Apple has already overdone it with the occasional re-confirmation of permissions on iPhone. For example, I've already given Citymapper access to my location so it can continue providing navigation in the background, so Apple, I really don't need you to ask me again whether I still want to keep this setting.

Yes, the strongest possible warning should be issued for Full Disk Access, but if someone chooses to grant this permission, macOS must respect their decision. Thank you, no more weekly or any form of mandatory re-confirmation.
